newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr to be range-bound in Asia after tankan tumult.
newsitem.headline: Dlr to be range-bound in Asia after tankan tumult.

text.p: The dollar is expected to be range-bound against the yen during Asian trade on Thursday, taking a breather after its tumble on Wednesday's release of the Bank of Japan's "tankan" survey, dealers said.
They said trade may be directionless unless fresh market-moving factors emerge.
"The dollar will be in a boxed range today with trade mostly directionless," a trust bank dealer said.
Some trust banks, probably on behalf of pension funds, may pick up dollars on dips and exporters will likely be interested in selling dollars near 115 yen, a city bank dealer said.

Dealers said an upbeat mood among major manufacturers shown in the tankan would keep the dollar's topside heavy. But they said a more pessimistic stance by non-manufacturers and small manufacturers had dimmed expectations of any imminent move by the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates, keeping traders reluctant to sell dollars aggressively.

A senior BOJ official said late on Wednesday that the Japanese economic recovery has not strengthened as much as the improvement in business sentiment among major manufacturers shown in the tankan. His comments led to short-covering of dollars in late trade.

Surging optimism among big Japanese manufacturers shown by the tankan suggested that Japan's huge trade surplus with the United States will continue to grow, which may fuel concerns over U.S.-Japan trade friction.
The trust bank dealer said Japanese investment trust firms were eager to sell dollars overnight. He said such demand for dollar sales may keep weighing on the dollar.

On Wednesday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said he saw no reason to expect concerted sales of U.S. Treasury securities and voiced confidence that U.S. markets could absorb them if they occurred.

"Our markets are so deep and so broad that even if there was enormous concerted selling by a foreign country -- I have no reason to think it would occur -- our markets could absorb it readily," Rubin told reporters.

His comments came two days after Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto seemed to suggest that Japan might be tempted to sell U.S. Treasuries and switch funds to gold if Washington did not cooperate with Tokyo to stabilise currencies.
In trade against the mark, the dollar is expected to be directionless, with some buying interst on dips supporting its downside, the city bank dealer said.
